title: A hand on Prahlada's head
hook: the hands that ended a tyrant rest on a child's head
carry: the fierce god's hand is a blessing
tomorrow: Prahlada's grandson takes heaven. who's the one left crying?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Prahlada turned down the Lord's offer, and Krishna's word in the Gita kept the askers in the circle too: bhakti asks nothing, yet every asker is welcome. Then the lion said: one wish, anyway.

A hand on the top of your head: a parent checking for fever, a grandparent's blessing, a coach after a loss. Go back to the moment Prahlada first bowed. The Bhagavata says Narasimha laid his hand on the boy's head, the same hand the gods had been too afraid to come near. Now the boy has one wish to spend. He doesn't spend it on himself. He spends it on his father.
screen: `A HAND ON THE HEAD.` → `THE HAND NO GOD WOULD APPROACH.` → `THE WISH: FOR HIS FATHER.`

segments.voice: His father. The king who tried every way to be rid of him, who struck the pillar to prove his son wrong. Prahlada asks Narasimha to free his father from the wrong he did to his own child. Not to pretend it didn't happen. To let it not stand against him. And Narasimha grants it, saying, in the telling, that the father is made pure because such a son was born in his family. Now come back to the hand. Raging, Narasimha frightened even the gods. Then a child bowed at his feet, and the Lord lifted him and laid a hand on his head. That's a blessing, and Hindu families still give it the same way. When a child bows and touches an elder's feet, the elder rests a hand on the child's head and blesses them: ashirvad. The fierce hand and the blessing hand are one hand. Temples show Narasimha both ways: fierce, ugra, in the doorway, and calm, sometimes with the goddess Lakshmi beside him. Devotees keep both, because his fierceness was never aimed at the child. It was protection. And the blessing ran further than anyone expected: through the boy, to the very father who had harmed him. That's how the Narasimha story closes. Not with claws. With a hand on a head.
screen: `THE WISH: FREE MY FATHER.` · `NOT ERASED. NOT HELD AGAINST HIM.` · `A HAND ON THE HEAD: A BLESSING.` · `FIERCE AND CALM, ONE LORD.` · then, large: `THE BLESSING REACHES HIS FATHER.`

segments.voice: Rest one palm lightly on the top of your head, the way an elder gives a blessing, and breathe slowly under it. If you pray, ask a blessing for someone who has been hard on you, the way Prahlada did for his father. If you don't, simply hold that person in mind, kindly, for a few breaths. And next time you greet an elder, notice the hand.
Narasimha: the man-lion, fierce toward harm, whose hand on Prahlada's head was a blessing.
The line: the fierce god's hand is a blessing, and Prahlada spent his one wish on his father. Rest well.

notes: Senses shape: touch (a hand on the head) carries the idea; the practice is a palm on the head or heart.
Confirm Bhagavata 7.9 (the hand on Prahlada's head, early in chapter 9) and 7.10.15–19 (the wish for the father; purified with his ancestors, the count left out). Paraphrased.
For parents: 'the father who tried to kill him' is said once, plainly; the chat gives an eight-year-old an answer about a fierce god.
Lakshmi-Narasimha images (calm, with Lakshmi beside or on his lap): standard iconography; confirm phrasing.
Surprising fact: the Narasimha story ends with a touch, and the child spends his one wish on the father who tried to kill him.
